title: Can a biased guess beat an honest one?
hook: One estimate is right on average. The other is deliberately off. Which misses by less?

knows: that averaging noisy readings gives an estimate
that a model can overfit noise
doesNotKnow: that average squared error splits into bias² plus spread²
that a deliberately biased estimate can have lower total error

misconception: An unbiased estimate is always the best one.
objective: The learner can explain that average squared error is bias² plus spread², so shrinking an estimate trades a little bias for much less spread and can lower the error, up to a point.

claims.text: With true value 0.5 and each estimate the average of 4 readings with noise sd 1, the plain average has bias 0, spread (sd) 0.5 and average squared error 0.25; half the average has bias −0.25, spread 0.25 and error 0.125.
claims.source: sd of a mean of 4 = 1/√4 = 0.5. For c × average: bias (c − 1)·0.5, sd 0.5c, error = bias² + sd². c = 1: 0.25; c = 0.5: 0.0625 + 0.0625 = 0.125. bias(), spread(), mse() in Demo.tsx. Brief 36 reports 200,000 simulated trials: 0.251 and 0.125.

claims.text: Shrinking too far costs more: at ×0.2 the bias is −0.40 and the error 0.170. The best factor here is exactly 0.5.
claims.source: mse(0.2) = 0.16 + 0.01 = 0.17. Minimising 0.25(1 − c)² + 0.25c² gives c = μ²/(μ² + σ²/n) = 0.25/0.5 = 0.5 (BEST in Demo.tsx).

claims.text: Average squared error is the average of the squared miss, and it equals bias squared plus variance (spread squared).
claims.source: Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., §7.3 (bias-variance decomposition).

claims.text: The setting is a toy and the 40 dots are sample estimates; the error readout is the long-run (expected) value, not computed from the 40 dots.
claims.source: Stage tag 'Toy · 40 sample estimates' and readout 'Long-run sq. error'. Dots from mulberry32(1) with Box-Muller normals, untuned, used only to show spread.

recall.question: A model's predictions are right on average but swing wildly from one data set to the next. Adding a penalty makes them a little biased but much steadier. What can happen to its average error?
options: It can go down, because spread shrinks more than bias grows
It must go up, because the model is now biased
It cannot change: bias and spread always cancel
recall.why: Average squared error is bias² plus spread². A small bias added for a big cut in spread can lower the total, until the bias grows too large.
